notes: All 69 electors who voted cast one of their two votes for George Washington, who became president. John Adams, second with 34, became vice president.
New York’s legislature failed to appoint its 8 electors in time, so New York cast no electoral votes. North Carolina and Rhode Island took no part because they had not yet ratified the Constitution.
Two Maryland electors did not vote, leaving 4 votes blank. In Virginia one elector did not vote and none was chosen in the 9th district, leaving another 4 blank.
In Massachusetts and New Hampshire voters cast ballots for electors, but the legislatures made the final choice. In New Jersey the governor and council chose the electors.

Voters chose between Federalist and Anti-Federalist elector slates, both expected to back Washington. All 33,460 popular votes, 26,299 for Federalist electors and 7,161 for Anti-Federalist electors, are counted for Washington.
The popular vote figures are incomplete estimates, and most New Hampshire townships are missing.

notes: All 132 electors who voted cast one of their two votes for George Washington, who was re-elected. John Adams, second with 77, was re-elected vice president.
Of the 135 electors appointed, two in Maryland and one in Vermont did not vote, leaving 4 votes blank in Maryland and 2 in Vermont.
In Massachusetts voters chose electors by majority vote in each district, and the legislature appointed the rest.
One Pennsylvania elector chosen on a Federalist slate voted for George Clinton instead of Adams. It is not clear whether this was a faithless vote.

Votes for both the Federalist slates (6,818) and the Democratic-Republican slates (962) are counted for Washington. Pennsylvania’s two leading electors, Joseph Hiester (3,396 votes) and William Henry (3,371), had both parties’ support, and only Hiester’s 3,396 is counted.
No Kentucky popular vote records are known. Virginia’s returns are incomplete, and only the Democratic-Republican figure survives.

notes: John Adams won with 71 electoral votes, one more than a majority of the 138 electors. Thomas Jefferson, second with 68, became vice president.
Some newspapers questioned the validity of Vermont’s electoral votes, but no objection was raised in Congress.

In Massachusetts each district’s voters elected an elector if someone won a majority, and the legislature chose the rest, along with two at large. In Tennessee three people named for each county elected the electors for each of the state’s three districts.
One Maryland elector pledged to Adams cast his two votes for Adams and Jefferson. Two electors, one in North Carolina and one in Virginia, voted for George Washington, who was not a candidate.

In each state the figures are for the most popular Adams elector and the most popular Jefferson elector, so the national totals are incomplete. The Massachusetts and Virginia figures also appear incomplete.
Kentucky and North Carolina chose electors by popular vote, but no popular vote figures are available for them.
Added up state by state, Adams has 32,967 votes. Wikipedia’s national table gives him 35,174, because it counts the Georgia and Maryland returns differently.

notes: Thomas Jefferson and Aaron Burr tied with 73 electoral votes each, so the House of Representatives chose between them, voting by state delegation. Jefferson became president and Burr vice president.
On the first 35 House ballots Jefferson won 8 states, Burr 6, and 2 were divided. On the 36th ballot, on February 17, 1801, Jefferson won 10 states to Burr’s 4, with 2 blank.
A 2004 analysis found that Georgia’s certificate of its electoral votes was not in the form the Constitution required. Its votes were counted for Jefferson and Burr without objection.

One Rhode Island Federalist elector voted for John Jay instead of Charles Cotesworth Pinckney so that Adams and Pinckney would not tie.

Votes for Democratic-Republican elector tickets are counted for Jefferson, and votes for Federalist tickets for Adams. The other 10 votes were cast in Maryland, 8 for electors pledged to both Adams and Jefferson and 2 for electors of unknown affiliation.

notes: This was the first election under the Twelfth Amendment, with each elector casting one vote for president and a separate vote for vice president. George Clinton was elected vice president with 162 electoral votes to 14 for Rufus King.

In the states with a popular vote, the Federalist elector tickets were formally unpledged. Their 39,245 votes appear as “Unpledged electors,” so Charles Cotesworth Pinckney has no popular vote of his own.
The unpledged electors who won Maryland’s 1st and 9th districts voted for Pinckney, as did the Federalist electors chosen by the Connecticut and Delaware legislatures.
The popular vote figures cover only 4 of North Carolina’s 14 districts and 1 of Tennessee’s 5. Some North Carolina district figures include votes rejected from the official count.
sourceNotes: In the popular-vote states the Federalist elector tickets were formally unpledged, and the article lists their 39245 popular votes as Unpledged electors (id unpledged, ev 0). In most states the article compares the most popular elector on each ticket; in the single-member districts of Maryland, North Carolina and Tennessee it sums the votes for electors pledged to each nominee; in Virginia the anti-Jefferson figure sums the leading electors of several tickets county by county.

notes: Indiana became a state on December 11, 1816, after the electors had met. An objection to counting its 3 electoral votes was postponed indefinitely, and they were counted.
Four electors did not vote: 1 in Delaware and the 3 Federalist electors chosen in Maryland’s 1st, 8th and 9th districts.

For vice president, Daniel D. Tompkins was elected with 183 electoral votes. The Federalist electors split theirs among John Eager Howard (22), James Ross (5), John Marshall (4) and Robert Goodloe Harper (3), and 4 votes were blank.
Rufus King was not formally nominated and did not campaign. His 34 electoral votes came from unpledged Federalist electors chosen by the legislatures of Connecticut, Delaware and Massachusetts.

The 17,300 votes for Federalist elector slates appear as Federalist “Unpledged electors,” so King has no popular vote of his own. In Pennsylvania an Independent ticket backed by disaffected Democratic-Republicans and Federalists received 17,597 votes and appears as Democratic-Republican “Unpledged electors.”
Returns are lost for 1 of Kentucky’s 3 districts and all 8 of Tennessee’s, so the popular vote is incomplete.

notes: Three electors pledged to Monroe, one each in Mississippi, Pennsylvania and Tennessee, died before the Electoral College met and were not replaced. As a result, 232 of the 235 electoral votes were cast.
Missouri’s statehood was disputed when the votes were counted, and Congress read the count both with and without its 3 electoral votes. They are included here, giving Monroe 231 rather than 228.

For vice president, Daniel D. Tompkins was re-elected with 218 electoral votes. Other electors gave Richard Stockton 8, Daniel Rodney 4, Robert Goodloe Harper 1 and Richard Rush 1, and 3 votes were not cast.
William Plumer, an elector from New Hampshire, voted for John Quincy Adams as a faithless elector.

The Federalists had no presidential candidate, and 14 of Monroe’s electoral votes came from Federalist electors in Delaware, Kentucky, Maryland and Massachusetts. In Massachusetts the Federalist slate won the popular vote, but its electors voted for Monroe.

notes: This was the first election in which Alaska and Hawaii took part, so 50 states cast electoral votes.
In Alabama, voters chose each of the 11 electors individually. Of the Democratic electors, 5 were pledged to Kennedy and 6 were unpledged.

Harry F. Byrd was not on the ballot but received 15 electoral votes: 6 from the unpledged Democratic electors chosen in Alabama, 8 from those chosen in Mississippi, and 1 from Henry D. Irwin, an Oklahoma elector pledged to Nixon. For vice president, the unpledged electors voted for Strom Thurmond, and Irwin voted for Barry Goldwater.

In Alabama, Kennedy is credited with the vote for his highest-polling elector (318,303) and the unpledged electors with 324,050, out of 570,225 ballots. Most Democratic voters chose electors from both slates, so Alabama’s shares add up to more than 100%.
For the same reason the national shares, counting Alabama’s votes for both slates, add up to a little more than 100%. Kennedy’s and Nixon’s shares are close to the usual figures, 49.72% and 49.55%.
Added up state by state, the unpledged electors have 610,409 votes. Wikipedia’s national table gives them 286,359, leaving out Alabama.
sourceNotes: Unpledged electors are listed as a candidate, despite under 1% of the national vote, because their slates won Mississippi and 6 Alabama electors.
